transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-10-04
Time: 08:42 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Marcus Lee (Cobalt VP Eng), Sonia Ramirez (NetOps), Daniel Cho (Security), Ellen Park (Platform)

Auto Summary (auto-generated, may be incomplete):
- Reviewed last week's canary where egress spike caused fallback to hosted cluster; discussed traffic shaping and circuit-breaker thresholds.
- Decided to try kernel-level scheduler flag + reduced batch window and re-run latency profiles.
- Security asked for KMS/HSM confirmation and audit-log retention clarification.
- Next steps: Redwood to share pricing/PS estimate and security pack; customer to run canary and upload results.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Alright, hey everyone, thanks for joining — I know it's early, appreciate it. Quick roll call — we're here to review the last week's pilot run, specifically the traffic surge profiling, the fallback event we saw, and the retuning plan. Priya you on?
[00:12] Priya Patel: Yep, hi all. Got the metrics pulled, I've got the traceroutes and p95/p99 breakdowns ready. I think the interesting part is how the egress burst coincided with longer KV cache warm ups.
[00:25] Marcus Lee: Morning. Quick context — we ran a synthetic load from our edge for 90 minutes yesterday and saw a sustained 2.4x increase in request rate starting at 02:14 UTC. Fallback happened around 02:16, correct?
[00:36] Priya Patel: Correct. The Redwood private canary node hit its configured circuit-breaker threshold at 02:16:08, so traffic routed to hosted. The p95 latency before fallback jumped from about 180ms to 620ms over the 90s window.
[00:50] Sonia Ramirez: And on our side we saw packet bursts and some retransmits — MTU unchanged, but we did see a lot more TCP retrans than normal. Not sure if that's net or something server-side.
[01:05] Daniel Cho: From security: we want to understand whether any fallback traffic touched any customer-only routes or ephemeral credentials — basically ensure we didn't leak any internal endpoints when you fell back to hosted.
[01:18] Alex Chen: Good call. Short answer: no internal endpoints were exposed. The fallback path uses the model gateway only, and we preserve tenancy headers. But we'll include the call trace and gateway logs in the packet we send.
[01:30] Ellen Park: Can you also include the exact request ids and timestamps? We need those to reconcile with our logging.
[01:36] Priya Patel: Yep, I'll bundle the request ids and the KV cache keys we saw warming. Note though transcription might show KV cash in the log, ignore that — it's KV cache.
[01:44] Marcus Lee: (laughs) yeah we've had the 'cash' typo for months.
[01:48] Alex Chen: Action item: Priya will post the traceroutes, gateway logs, and a timeline to the pilot doc. Priya, due?
[01:55] Priya Patel: I'll have initial artifacts up by EOD today.
[02:00] Marcus Lee: Cool. Can we walk through what the proposed mitigation is? We heard kernel flags mentioned in the doc — what's the practical impact?
[02:12] Priya Patel: Sure. Two knobs: one is the runtime kernel flag that reduces the token scheduler window — that reduces the batch accumulation time which lowers tail latency at the cost of slightly higher per-token CPU. Second is reducing the default circuit-breaker threshold and adding a short cool-down so we avoid oscillation.
[02:30] Alex Chen: To be explicit, the test set is: kernel flag on canary host + batch window from 25ms to 12ms + circuit-breaker threshold down 20%. We'll run the same synthetic profile and compare p50/p95/p99 and unit cost.
[02:45] Sonia Ramirez: When you do that, can you also test egress shaping from our side? We can cap egress to the private pool to simulate constrained paths.
[02:53] Priya Patel: Yes — please do that. It helps us reproduce the retrans behavior.
[03:00] Daniel Cho: On the security front — two things. One: KMS integration — are you using customer-managed keys in this pilot? Two: audit log retention and whether logs include PII or sensitive tokens.
[03:12] Alex Chen: We're currently using Redwood-managed keys for the pilot but customer-managed keys (CMK) via KMS are supported on Private. For PII, we redact request bodies in the stored telemetry and include an option to disable storing payloads entirely. We'll send the exact config options.
[03:26] Daniel Cho: Okay please send the KMS integration notes, and if HSM is required for us we'll have to flag that to procurement.
[03:33] Alex Chen: Noted. We'll include the HSM path and the difference in the SOW.
[03:38] Marcus Lee: Back to the failure — was the fallback immediate to hosted or was there a grace window?
[03:45] Priya Patel: There's a brief 10-second grace to allow KV warm-up. After that, if the median queue depth exceeds the threshold for two consecutive windows, we trip and route to hosted. In yesterday's run the warm-up plus build-up caused the threshold to be crossed sooner than expected.
[03:58] Ellen Park: Is that 10-second grace configurable from the customer's side?
[04:02] Priya Patel: Yes, in Private you can set the grace and the circuit-breaker policy. For Dedicated we've seen customers want tighter control, and we provide RBAC controls around policy changes.
[04:12] Marcus Lee: Could we get a recommended starting policy for our traffic pattern? Our bursts are 1–3 minutes long typically.
[04:20] Priya Patel: We'll recommend a staging policy: 15s grace, circuit-breaker threshold at 1.6x baseline, and adaptive cool-down of 30s. We'll put the numbers and runbooks in the doc.
[04:30] Alex Chen: Another ask from us: can you produce packet captures from both AZs and one internal edge so we can correlate retransmits with server logs? It fast-tracks root cause.
[04:40] Sonia Ramirez: Yep we'll capture and upload. Expect those by tomorrow morning.
[04:45] (short pause)
[05:00] Priya Patel: Quick note on quantization — we rolled a small change two weeks ago that slightly changed memory layout; in rare cases that can affect kernel scheduling. We're not saying it's the root cause but it's in the list of suspects. We'll test with and without the quant stack on the canary.
[05:17] Marcus Lee: Let us know if that's reversible quickly because we can revert easily from our side.
[05:22] Priya Patel: Should be reversible, yes.
[05:25] Daniel Cho: Regarding logging and compliance: what's the retention window for the pilot logs? We need at least 90 days for audit.
[05:32] Alex Chen: Pilot defaults to 30 days but enterprise tiers can be configured for 90+; we can bump retention for this pilot per request and share cost impact. That'll be included in the PS estimate.
[05:42] Marcus Lee: Perfect. One other question: if fallback touches hosted, do you preserve customer routing policies like allowlists?
[05:50] Priya Patel: Yes, the hosted fallback uses the customer's network ruleset and allowlist. We don't create open inbound endpoints. However, if you'd locked down some routes in your VPC that the hosted path doesn't have access to, that could change behavior; we'll document that explicitly.
[06:05] (background noise, someone typing)
[06:20] Alex Chen: Let's talk metrics we want to compare: p50/p95/p99 latency, request per second throughput, egress bytes, token cost per 1k, and failover frequency. Also measure cold-starts and KV cache miss rate during the surge.
[06:36] Priya Patel: Already instrumented those. I've added a column for KV hit ratio per minute. The heatmap shows the warm period aligned with cache miss increases.
[06:45] Marcus Lee: In the spreadsheet please flag the exact timestamps, we need to map to our logs.
[06:49] Priya Patel: Will do.
[06:50] Marcus Lee: Thanks.
[06:53] Alex Chen: Competitors question — Marcus had asked about Bedrock or a Triton self-hosted bench. Any insights?
[06:58] Marcus Lee: We're evaluating a Triton stack internally for some models but the integration and ops cost looked higher. We wanted to be sure Redwood can give us predictable SLAs.
[07:07] Priya Patel: That's the trade-off — self-hosting can be cheaper per-token if you optimize thoroughly but the ops overhead and fallback complexity go up. We're focusing on minimizing that ops friction for Private.
[07:18] Daniel Cho: Another security note: would you be able to provide network flow logs in a consumable format that ties to our internal SIEM? JSON events ideally.
[07:26] Alex Chen: Yes, we can ship flow logs as JSON and provide a small mapping doc for your SIEM. We'll coordinate with Ellen on field names.
[07:34] Ellen Park: Please include examples so we can test ingestion.
[07:38] Alex Chen: Will do.
[07:40] (brief pause)
[08:00] Priya Patel: Ok, on the retune plan — test matrix is: baseline run (yesterday config), kernel flag + reduced batch window, kernel flag + reduced batch window + reduced circuit-breaker threshold, and a quick rollback case where we revert quantization to see diffs. We'll run each for 20 minutes with the same synthetic spike.
[08:20] Marcus Lee: Can you also include a run with our egress shaping set to 70% of normal so we know how it behaves under constrained egress?
[08:27] Priya Patel: Good call — yes we'll add that.
[08:30] Alex Chen: We'll schedule the runs over the next two days; Priya will run them from Redwood side and Sonia will concurrently run the egress-shaped test from Cobalt.
[08:39] Sonia Ramirez: Sounds good. I'll coordinate a time window and share host IPs for captures.
[08:44] Daniel Cho: One last security question: are any tokens or credentials stored in plaintext in transit to hosted during fallback?
[08:50] Priya Patel: No. All creds are short-lived and forwarded using signed headers; payloads are TLS-encrypted end-to-end. We'll include the header mapping in the security pack.
[08:59] Marcus Lee: Ok thanks.
[09:02] Alex Chen: Great. I want to call out two risks: 1) repeated fallback oscillation could double our unit cost if not tuned, and 2) packet retrans patterns might point to an infra-level mismatch we need to fix, not just policy. So we should plan for a quick rollback path.
[09:18] Priya Patel: For rollback, we've got canary images pinned and a rollback playbook that Priya can run — it'll take ~10 minutes to switch the kernel flags back and restart the runtime.
[09:28] Marcus Lee: Do you do canary traffic splitting natively or do we need to stitch on our side?
[09:33] Priya Patel: Redwood can do route percentage splits by customer, but for pilot-level control we often ask customers to trigger the synthetic traffic from their side while we observe. It's more deterministic.
[09:43] Alex Chen: Let's pick a time tomorrow at 02:00 UTC for the first retune run. Priya, can you own it?
[09:49] Priya Patel: I can. I'll schedule and send calendar invite.
[09:52] Marcus Lee: Works for us.
[09:55] (crosstalk)
[10:10] Ellen Park: Quick procurement question — we may need a short term dedicated pool if fallback frequency is high. How quickly can you stand up a small Dedicated test pool for us?
[10:19] Alex Chen: We can provision a tiny dedicated pool in 7–10 days for testing; for production it takes longer. I'll include a pricing estimate.
[10:27] Marcus Lee: Ok include the 7-day estimate and monthly commit numbers.
[10:31] Alex Chen: Noted.
[10:34] (pause)
[10:55] Priya Patel: One small item — during the last run we saw an anomalous spike in GPU memory pressure on host rdx-07. I'm running memory flamegraphs now. Could be unrelated but wanted to flag.
[11:07] Marcus Lee: If we get the flamegraphs can we do a quick pairing session to interpret?
[11:12] Priya Patel: Absolutely. I'll ping your team when available.
[11:16] Daniel Cho: Also flagging that if kernel flags cause any perf regressions we want a rollback within a single maintenance window — document that in the playbook.
[11:24] Alex Chen: Will do.
[11:28] (typing)
[11:40] Alex Chen: Ok let's recap — Priya posts logs + request ids today; Sonia uploads pcaps tomorrow morning; Priya runs kernel + batch window tests and posts results by 2027-10-08; Alex to share pricing + SOC2/security pack by 2027-10-06; Marcus will run canary from their side at the scheduled 02:00 UTC slot and report. Any other items?
[11:59] Marcus Lee: One ask — include a note on expected unit cost delta when you lower the batch window. I know you said it increases CPU per token — give us % range.
[12:09] Alex Chen: We'll provide ballpark: expect 5–15% token cost increase depending on model size and sequence length. We'll quantify it in the PS doc.
[12:18] Ellen Park: Also please add example SIEM mappings and sample JSON flow logs.
[12:24] Alex Chen: Yes.
[12:26] (brief silence)
[12:36] Daniel Cho: Final sec question — if we go to CMK, is key rotation supported without downtime?
[12:42] Priya Patel: Key rotation is supported and we'll do a staged rewrap process to avoid downtime; we'll provide the runbook.
[12:49] Alex Chen: Alright, if there's nothing else we'll wrap. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts and calendar invites.
[13:00] Marcus Lee: Thanks all.
[13:03] (call ends)
